sections.normalized_html: An oil tank has leaked [MATH: q(t)] liters of oil after [MATH: t] hours. The graph of [MATH: q(t)] is shown below. Approximate the rate at which the oil is leaking from the tank when [MATH: t=1] using a forward difference approximation with step size [MATH: h=1.]

An oil tank has leaked [MATH: q(t)] liters of oil after [MATH: t] hours. The graph of [MATH: q(t)] is shown below. Approximate the rate at which the oil is leaking from the tank when [MATH: t=1] using a forward difference approximation with step size [MATH: h=1.]

[IMG: /graphics/b42fd1d22af4ee74a06a5344ab52a8c8]

sections.normalized_html:
We use the forward difference approximation [MATH: q'(t) \approx \frac{q(t+h) - q(t)}{h}]

at the time [MATH: t=1] with step size [MATH: h=1.] This gives

[MATH: q^{′}(1)|≈ (q(1 + 1) − q(1))/(1); = (q(2) − q(1))/(1); = 3 − 2; = 1.]

So, after [MATH: 1] hour, the tank is leaking oil at a rate of approximately [MATH: 1\,\textrm{liter}/ \textrm{hour}.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
For a function [MATH: f(x),] its derivative at a point [MATH: x] is defined by the limit
[MATH: f'(x) = \lim\limits_{h\to 0} \frac{f(x+h) - f(x) }{h}.]
But often, computing this limit exactly is impossible or impractical. One example might be when we don't have an explicit expression for [MATH: f(x).] In such cases, instead of finding an exact value for [MATH: f'(x)], we can approximate the derivative using the formula

Content:
[MATH: f'(x)\approx \frac{f(x+h) - f(x) }{h}]

Content:
for small values of the "step size" [MATH: h,] with [MATH: h>0.]

Content:
This expression is called the forward difference approximation because if [MATH: h >0] then [MATH: x+h] is a step forward (i.e., to the right) from [MATH: x.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/58c0fc28ed1e2bb0698d1789623d448e]

Content:
Generally, this and other similar methods are known as finite-difference approximations. The smaller the value of [MATH: h,] the better the approximation.

---

Item 2 — Example: Estimating a Derivative From a Table Using a Forward Difference Approximation

Example Prompt:
A function [MATH: f(x)] has values according to the table below:

| [MATH: x] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 3] | [MATH: 4] | [MATH: 5] | [MATH: 6] | [MATH: 7] |
| [MATH: f(x)] | [MATH: -1.0] | [MATH: -0.7] | [MATH: -0.3] | [MATH: 0.7] | [MATH: 1.5] | [MATH: 2.1] |

Approximate at the point [MATH: x=3] using a forward difference approximation.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We use the forward difference approximation formula
[MATH: f'(x) \approx \frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h}]

at the point [MATH: x=3.] We choose the step size [MATH: h] to be as small as possible, in this case [MATH: h=1.] This gives

[MATH: f^{′}(3)|≈ (f(3 + 1) − f(3))/(1); = (f(4) − f(3))/(1); = ((− 0.3) − (− 0.7))/(1); = (0.4)/(1); = 0.4.]

Explanation:
We use the forward difference approximation
[MATH: s'(t) \approx \frac{s(t+h) - s(t)}{h}]
